Photograph: Jon Nazca/Reuters View image in fullscreen Police officers and Spanish soldiers escorting people in Ceuta to the border with Morocco on Saturday morning. Photograph: Jon Nazca/Reuters Spain Spanish PM calls for urgent EU meeting after ‘selfish’ responses to Ceuta crisis Pedro Sánchez hits out at ‘polarising and unlawful reaction’ over mass crossing into Spanish enclave in north Africa Europe live – latest updates Sam Jones in Madrid and Lisa O’Carroll in London Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.35 EDT First published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 06.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , has called for an urgent meeting of EU interior ministers after what he called some member states’ “selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction” to this week’s mass border crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, in north Africa. More than 50,000 people crossed into the territory from Morocco on Thursday and Friday, with at least 67 people dying in the attempt. Some drowned, while others were crushed as they tried to cross a breakwater barrier. Although more than 48,000 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday, the influx triggered a political crisis for the Madrid government and led some fellow EU countries to call for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Sánchez confirmed “virtually all” of those who had crossed the border had been returned, “preventing any unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe”. However, he asked for the meeting after what appeared to be a breakdown of EU unity on external border policy, with Italy attacking Spain . Italy announced on Friday evening that it would suspend its Schengen arrangements with Spain for a month, even though Ceuta – and Spain’s other north African enclave, Melilla – are subject to special Schengen rules that prevent onward movement within the zone. Map showing location of Ceuta in Mediterranean region, and another showing location of Tarajal breakwater on border between Ceuta and Morocco Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now-closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”. Sánchez was forthright in a letter sent to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Council president, António Costa, and Micheál Martin, the prime minister of Ireland, which holds the EU presidency. View image in fullscreen Pedro Sánchez speaking at a press conference in Ceuta on Friday. Photograph: Borja Puig de la Bellacasa/Moncloa handout/EPA Sánchez said that while most EU countries had expressed support and solidarity over events in Ceuta, others had chosen to attack Spain. “Such an attitude – driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest – is … contrary to European law, humanitarian law, and the principles of solidarity that bind us together,” he said. In a pointed rebuke to Italy, he noted that Spain was “according to Frontex, one of the least porous external borders of the European Union , with a number of irregular entries that is half that recorded, for example, in Italy in recent years (2021–2026)”. He concluded by saying the EU could not afford “this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction” and asked for an urgent video conference of EU interior ministers to address the issue. Senior EU officials are due to meet on Saturday in a “political crisis response team” convened by Ireland’s presidency. 3:37 Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - video Ireland’s justice minister, Jim O’Callaghan, who is leading the meeting on behalf of the EU, said he had been in touch with Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, to express his solidarity and support. “I will remain in close contact with the Spanish government, member states and the EU institutions as the situation evolves,” he said on Friday night. France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said his country would not be seeking Spain’s suspension from Schengen rules. “It’s absolutely not on the table,” he said on Saturday. “We have great cooperation with Spain.” Many of the remaining people who crossed into Ceuta returned to Morocco on Saturday morning amid a reinforced Spanish police and military presence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Preview latest after newsletter promotion “We hope to go to Europe to work and earn a living – that’s it,” Souleil Boyan, a 19-year-old from Senegal, told Agence France-Presse outside a migrant centre in Ceuta where dozens of other people from sub-Saharan Africa were waiting for officials. “We all know that in Africa there isn’t much opportunity,” he added. The Spanish government said in a statement on Saturday that the situation in Ceuta remained calm and quiet. “Friday night passed without incident,” it said. “Entries were completely halted, while departures to Morocco continued without any notable events.” It said containment barriers were being installed at the Tarajal beach breakwater, including a 500-metre-long inflatable barrier and a line of anchored buoys. This week’s mass crossing dwarfs the last similar event in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over two days. That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania. That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara, a move that caused a rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group. Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria. The Spanish government has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned under special rules. But some migration experts have expressed doubts about that explanation. Mauricio Valiente, the director general of the Spanish Refugee Aid Commission, said the route into Ceuta was very different from the Atlantic route from Africa to the Canary Islands , which is often operated by people smugglers. “Unlike what happens in the Canary Islands, these aren’t people who have to get into a small boat,” he told elDiario.es . “This is a matter of being just metres from a land border, jumping into the sea and trying to get around a breakwater, which makes it much easier to do, even with all the risks.” Valiente said there had been a steady increase in arrivals to Ceuta this year, even before the supreme court ruling. “The causes are complex, and there are surely many reasons,” he said. “But to simplify it by referencing the court ruling or organised crime – to say there’s a direct cause-and-effect relationship – is completely unfounded.” Explore more on these topics Spain Europe European Union Morocco Migration Pedro Sánchez Africa news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Live Spain leaving Schengen ‘not on table’ says France after Sánchez hits out at EU response to Ceuta crisis – Europe live Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco? https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/uk-news/mu.text: A mum was so terrified of flying she deliberately lost her boarding pass for a family holiday - only to sob when helpful airport staff gave her another. Debbie Adamson suffers from aerophobia, an intense fear of being on an aeroplane, which affects approximately one in 10 people. The retired headteacher says at its worst she once hid her boarding pass in a WHSmith magazine at Gatwick airport in a desperate attempt to avoid flying to Orlando, Florida, with her 'theme park addict' husband and three kids. The 67-year-old says she 'didn't care' even when her kids started sobbing but when airline staff simply printed her another one so she could still fly she was left 'crying solid' for three hours. Her phobia started during the 'world's worst flight' from Budapest when she was a student that left her terrified that every airplane she got on was going to crash. However, she forced herself on eight trips to Disneyland Florida with her family but says cabin crew would have to console her 'howling' and she had to hold her husband tightly. Finally she decided she 'couldn't do it' anymore and quit flying for 17 years in 2008. After learning how planes worked from a pilot pal and joining a Facebook support group, she decided to book a trip to Santorini to celebrate her 40th wedding anniversary in 2025. After learning more about her phobia, Debbie discovered that listening to a playlist of her favourite songs by Korean boyband BTS helped calm her sensory overload. Focusing on the 'bulletproof' list of K-pop hits allowed her to fly to Orlando in Florida, US, again last year where she 'didn't bat an eyelid' even during turbulence. Now she hopes to spread awareness about her phobia to encourage others to 'give themselves permission to not be frightened'. Debbie, from Southampton, Hampshire, said: "When I was a student I flew to Budapest and we had the world's worst flight, it was my first flight and I was on my own. When we landed it bounced down the wrong way and there were sparks coming off the wing tips and it was lurching. It was your horror come true. "From that point onwards I thought every aeroplane I ever got on was going to crash. It was shocking and it was horrible. After that I didn't want to go anywhere on a plane ever again, I was terrified. I then went and married a theme park addict and I made myself go on those flights for my family. It was the flight crew that was my coping strategy. "When I had to fly during this terrified period, I would tell the stewardess [about my phobia] when I went through the door if I wasn't [already] crying. My husband used to come off every flight with permanent arthritis in his hands where I'd be holding onto him so tightly. "I can't explain it, you just can't control it. It's just abject terror, it's ridiculous. Even the slightest hint of turbulence I'd be crying again if I stopped. I never ate or drank, I came off flights feeling quite unwell. It was really quite bad. "One time I was sitting at the airport and said 'I need to go into the bathroom'. I veered into WH Smith and I had my boarding pass with me and I put it in a girly magazine where I thought no one would ever look on the top shelf. "I came weeping back saying 'I've lost my boarding pass, I can't go'. My kids all started crying. We got to an airline representative and said 'can you help, she's lost her boarding pass?'. There I was thinking they'd say 'she's got to go home' but they printed me another one. "I cried solid for at least three hours. I got onto that plane with dehydration I cried so much. I still did it though, it never got worse than that." Debbie revealed that she started learning how planes worked from her pilot pal and joined a Facebook support group to learn more about overcoming her phobia. After 17 years of refusing to fly she decided to book a trip to Santorini where she says she discovered that listening to her favourite boyband BTS helped to calm her sensory overload. Debbie said: "I'd always wanted to go to Santorini but I thought 'can I even face it?' My partner was pleasantly surprised when I suggested the Santorini trip. If I could pinpoint one thing, taking out the sensory overload was what changed it. I sat there with every sense bombarding me with distressing information. "So I thought I'd take two out and I made a bulletproof playlist - every single track I love so that I knew I'd keep listening. I shut my eyes during take-off and I also held on very tightly too, once I did that I began to rationalise it. "It just proved to myself that I gave myself permission not to be frightened anymore so I wasn't. All the pressure was put on me by my own mind. On the way back from the trip to Orlando the pilot said it was going to be a bumpy flight and it was and I didn't bat an eyelid. "Just as the first big bump came, Bruce Springsteen started playing on the movie I was just watching, and it was 'Born in the USA'. The plane went 'boom' and I just laughed. I'm completely different. [I was] bouncing along to the Bruce Springsteen film, whereas before I would've been crying my head off with stewardesses on either side of me trying to calm me down. "It can be quite disarming when someone's howling." Now Debbie says she is looking to book more trips in the future and hopes to spread awareness about her experience to help others living with the phobia. Debbie said: "I'd never say I'm cured but having that self-awareness to think 'I'm going to take out those three senses and I'm going to give myself permission to not be frightened'. "It wasn't anything to be ashamed of, I couldn't help it, but what I hadn't done was to allow my mind the freedom to find out about this and be a bit more logical about this. It's understandable to feel like that but you don't have to and you can choose not to. It sounds so easy but it's so hard to do. I feel changed. It opens up a whole new vista."

https://english.news.cn/20260822/4581f66.text: Roundup: Polish experts see growing potential for AI cooperation with China Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-08-22 22:49:45 WARSAW, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) moves rapidly from laboratories into factories, hospitals and classrooms, its expanding applications are creating new opportunities for scientific and technological cooperation between China and Poland. Polish experts see growing potential for deeper China-Poland AI cooperation, citing the complementary strengths of China's mature industrial ecosystem and broad application market and Poland's expertise in mathematics, engineering and basic research. Katarzyna Kaniewska, an official with the Foreign Cooperation Office of the Polish Chamber of Commerce, said China and Poland can deepen cooperation in healthcare, climate-related services and education. Both China and Europe face population aging and declining birth rates. AI can help ease pressure on healthcare systems by handling some routine examinations, laboratory tests and administrative tasks, allowing medical professionals to devote more time to work requiring human judgment, Kaniewska said. It can also support climate monitoring and early warning, while serving as an auxiliary tool for teachers and students, she added. For companies, cooperation can help develop AI solutions tailored to local market demand. For researchers, it can expand existing personnel exchanges into joint work in basic research, said Roman Szewczyk, director of the Systems Research Institute of the Polish Academy of Sciences. Cezary Blaszczyk, director of the Department of International Cooperation at the National Centre for Research and Development of Poland, said Chinese and Polish researchers have shown a strong willingness to work together and that the potential for AI cooperation is substantial. According to Szewczyk, basic research should remain central to AI cooperation. His institute has trained doctoral students from China, and he hopes collaboration can expand beyond personnel exchanges to joint fundamental research. Krzysztof Pyrc, president of the Foundation for Polish Science, said the potential of research cooperation with China remains underestimated by some scientists abroad. Greater links among universities, research institutes, funding bodies and enterprises can help convert complementary strengths into concrete results, he said. For China and Poland, robotics cooperation can bring together AI algorithms, sensors, control systems, mechatronics and manufacturing expertise, creating opportunities in areas ranging from industrial automation to medical and elderly-care services. The benefits, however, will extend beyond robotics. The same model -- joint research followed by local testing and adaptation -- can be applied in healthcare, climate services and education. It can also make AI tools more accessible to Polish small and medium-sized enterprises, helping them improve efficiency and develop new products and services. Blaszczyk emphasized that companies generally approach cooperation in practical terms, focusing on technological strengths, product competitiveness and market demand. Such an approach can help turn scientific collaboration into viable products and services with wider economic and social value. "I hope the challenges brought by AI development can be addressed through bilateral cooperation, and that AI can benefit humanity and create more possibilities for future cooperation," said Blaszczyk. ■

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text: Art law news Challenges mounting to US laws enacted to aid recovery of Nazi-looted art The Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection Foundation in Madrid and the Norton Simon Museum in California are pushing back against recent statutes related to Holocaust-era expropriation claims Martha Lufkin 28 October 2026 Share Camille Pissarro's Rue Saint-Honoré, dans l'après-midi. Effet de pluie (1897), at the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid, has been the subject of a Nazi-loot restitution claim in California for decades Photo © The Art Newspaper Reopened claims in California are testing new laws that were enacted to counteract court decisions in favour of museums in Nazi-looted art cases. The California and US federal statutes, which change the procedural rules for Nazi-looted art claims, are being challenged by the Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection Foundation (TBCF) in Madrid, and the Norton Simon Museum (NSM) in Pasadena, California. Both museums are facing new litigation in art ownership claims that were previously decided in their favour by court judgments which both Congress and the California legislature cited negatively as reasons for changing the law. The challenges by the museum and foundation now launch the statutes towards court judgment themselves as to their permissibility. On 19 October, Judge John Walter of the federal district court in Los Angeles said he would issue a decision in the TBCF case without oral argument, based on the submitted briefs. The museum and plaintiffs have each moved for summary judgment in the reconsideration of a claim to recover a Nazi-looted painting by Camille Pissarro, which had already been adjudicated in favour of TBCF. Art law US Supreme Court sends dispute over Nazi-looted Pissarro back to California court, reopening door for restitution claim Martha Lufkin The reconsideration was ordered in 2025 by the US Supreme Court , after California amended its procedural laws in 2024 to aid state residents who sue museums for stolen works of art. The legislature criticised a 2022 Ninth Circuit federal court of appeals decision which said Spanish property law applied to the TBCF case, and that under the Spanish “acquisitive prescription” principle, TBCF owned the painting. The work is Pissarro’s Rue Saint Honoré, apres midi, effect de pluie (1897). The Supreme Court vacated the decision because under California’s new procedural statute, California’s substantive law, and no one else’s, applies in claims for stolen art at museums, regardless of prior judicial decisions. The plaintiffs, David Cassirer and other heirs of the original owner, Lilly Neubauer, justify recovery of the painting because Neubauer, a Jew based in Berlin, was forced in 1939 to sell it to Nazis to obtain an exit visa, and was not allowed to access the payment. In the renewed proceedings, Neubauer’s heirs argue that under the new California rule, California’s property law applies, “under which good title can never be acquired to stolen property”. The painting therefore must be returned to them as rightful owners. The plaintiffs also cite a second legislative change, which followed soon after California’s: the amendment by the US Congress of the federal Holocaust Era Art Recovery (Hear) Act. The amendment took effect in April 2026 and was expressly applicable to pending lawsuits. For Nazi-loot claims that it covers, the new Hear Act bars art possessors from relying on “defences or substantive doctrines based on the passage of time”, including “acquisitive prescription”. The prior court proceedings had found that TBCF earned ownership of the painting under Spanish acquisitive prescription, because TBCF possessed the painting for more than six years without actually knowing it was stolen. The plaintiffs say that the 2025 Hear Act’s bar of any reliance on acquisitive prescription thus “conclusively resolves” all issues in their favour. But the TBCF is challenging the new statutes. It says that the California law violates the US constitution by retroactively denying it of its vested property rights in the painting without due process, and that the Hear Act, if applied to this case to achieve that, will be unconstitutional too. Acquisitive prescription is not a “defence based on the passage of time”, but a property vesting law under the substantive law of Spain, it says, and prior court decisions in the case repeatedly found that TBCF’s property rights vested no later than 1999, “more than twenty-six years before the [Hear] Act’s enactment”. The TBCF makes multiple other challenges to the new laws, including that the new California law is an impermissible state attempt to regulate conduct extraterritorially in Spain. The governments of the United States and California have intervened in the lawsuit, submitting briefs defending the constitutionality of their statutes. Friend of the court briefs have also been filed on both sides. A decision is expected likely by late February. ucas Cranach the Elder, Adam and Eve (around 1530) In the second lawsuit, the NSM on 14 October challenged a complaint filed in September in state court and removed it to the federal district court in Los Angeles. The claimants seek recovery of a diptych, Adam and Eve (around 1530), by Lucas Cranach the Elder. The paintings were among 800 works stolen from the Old Masters dealership in the Netherlands owned by Jacques Goudstikker, a Dutch Jew, by Nazi Reichsmarschall Hermann Göring in 1940. Prior litigation seeking the Cranach diptych ended in a judgment for the museum. In 2018, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed the case based on the “act of state” doctrine, under which the actions of the Dutch government within its borders, including its allegedly wrongful sale of the Cranach paintings to a third party, cannot be adjudicated by US courts. The prior litigation was brought by Marei von Saher, Goudstikker’s sole surviving heir. The current lawsuit relies on the new California law allowing new claims even if previously dismissed on procedural grounds, and is brought by Von Saher’s assignees, Daniel Gryczman and the Jewish Federation Council of Greater Los Angeles. The NSM is telling the court that the new lawsuit is a “misguided and meritless” action seeking to relieve the museum from its prior judgment, and is requesting a permanent injunction precluding the re-litigation. The prior judgment dismissed Von Saher’s claims “on the merits” andquieted NSM’s title to the Cranach diptych, the museum’s representatives say, and it asks the court to grant its requests to spare it “the open-ended threat of future litigation”. Art law Two Nazi loot claims may test California statute intended to remove roadblocks to restitution Martha Lufkin A third lawsuit is also unfolding based on the new California law. In it, the daughters of the Czech Jewish artist Dina Gottliebova Babbitt are seeking recovery from the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum (ABM) in Poland of portraits Babbitt was forced to create while imprisoned at the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp. Under the process required to sue a foreign government instrumentality, the museum, an instrumentality of Poland, has not yet been joined to the case, a representative for the ABM tells The Art Newspaper , and has not yet filed a response. Babbitt’s daughters filed their complaint in September. The Hear Act amendment is also being tested in other federal courts. One of the cases, brought against Austria and two Austrian museums in the federal district court for the Southern District of New York, is considering the constitutionality of the Hear Act’s denial of otherwise applicable defences.
